source_refs.note: Practice MCQs written from Chapter 18 (PDF 118-136, printed 114-132); not printed in the book. Based on the chapter's text, tables, boxes and worked examples (numericals with changed values); none repeats the chapter exercise. Drafts needing academic review.

blocks.text: Practice MCQs for the whole of Chapter 18 (Quantum Physics), arranged by the chapter's sections. Each question has one correct answer with a short explanation; numerical questions show the working.

blocks.prompt: 1 Quantum theory assumes that electromagnetic radiation behaves as:

options.text: a uniform field carrying no energy

blocks.explanation: Quantum theory treats electromagnetic radiation as discrete packets of energy (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: Quantum Theory assumes the behaviour of electromagnetic radiations as discrete packets of energy

blocks.prompt: 2 According to the chapter, classical physics:

options.text: is still valid in ordinary processes of everyday life

blocks.explanation: Classical physics is still valid in ordinary processes of everyday life; quantum theory is needed on a very small scale (Introduction).

book_ref.quote: the classical physics is still valid in ordinary processes of everyday life

blocks.prompt: 3 Max Planck suggested that energy is radiated or absorbed:

options.text: only in the form of electrons

blocks.explanation: Planck suggested that energy is radiated or absorbed in discrete packets called quanta rather than as a continuous wave (18.1).

book_ref.quote: In 1901, Max Planck suggested that energy is radiated or absorbed in discrete packets of energy called quanta

blocks.prompt: 4 A quantum is:

options.text: a particle of matter with rest mass

blocks.explanation: Quanta is the plural of quantum, which is a discrete packet of energy (18.1).

book_ref.quote: Quanta is plural of quantum, a discrete packet of energy.

blocks.prompt: 5 Each quantum is associated with radiation of:
blocks.explanation: Each quantum is associated with radiation of a single frequency, and its energy is E = hf (18.1).

book_ref.quote: Each quantum is associated with radiations of a single frequency.

blocks.prompt: 6 The value of Planck's constant h is:
blocks.explanation: Planck's constant h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s (18.1).

book_ref.quote: where h is Planck's constant, its value is 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s.

blocks.prompt: 7 What is the energy of one quantum of radiation of frequency 6 × 10¹⁴ Hz?

book_ref.quote: The energy E of each quantum is proportional to its frequency f related as

blocks.prompt: 8 Two photons have wavelengths 400 nm and 800 nm. The ratio of their energies E₄₀₀ : E₈₀₀ is:
blocks.explanation: E = hf = hc/λ, so E ∝ 1/λ. Halving the wavelength doubles the energy: E₄₀₀ : E₈₀₀ = 800 : 400 = 2 : 1 (18.1).

book_ref.quote: The energy E of each quantum is proportional to its frequency f related as

blocks.prompt: 9 Max Planck received the Nobel Prize in physics for his discovery of energy quanta in:
blocks.explanation: Planck received the Nobel Prize in 1918 (18.1). 1921 was Einstein, 1927 Compton, 1932 Heisenberg.

book_ref.quote: Max Planck received Nobel Prize in physics in 1918 for his discovery of energy quanta.

blocks.prompt: 10 Which constant is described in the chapter as a constant of the special theory of relativity?
blocks.explanation: h is the constant of quantum theory and c, the speed of light, is the constant of special relativity (18.1, box).

book_ref.quote: another important constant c is the speed of light c which is a constant of special theory of relativity

blocks.prompt: 11 Einstein called the indivisible tiny bundles of energy of electromagnetic radiation:
blocks.explanation: Einstein called these indivisible bundles photons; a beam of light is a stream of photons travelling at speed c (18.1).

book_ref.quote: These indivisible tiny bundles of energy he called

blocks.prompt: 12 Planck assumed that the particle nature of radiation from hot bodies was due to:

options.text: the speed of light in air
some property of the atoms producing it
the colour of the hot body's surface
the pressure of the surrounding gas

blocks.explanation: Planck assumed the granular nature of radiation from hot bodies came from some property of the atoms producing it (18.1).

book_ref.quote: He assumed that granular or particle nature of radiation from hot bodies was due to some property of the atoms producing it.

blocks.prompt: 13 The energy E and momentum p of a photon are related by:
blocks.explanation: From E = mc² and p = mc, E = pc (Eq. 18.2).

book_ref.quote: From the theory of relativity E = mc², the relativistic momentum of photon is; p = mc,

blocks.prompt: 14 The momentum of a photon of wavelength λ is:
blocks.explanation: pc = hf gives p = hf/c; since c = fλ, p = h/λ (Eq. 18.3). hc/λ is the photon's energy, not its momentum.

book_ref.quote: From the theory of relativity E = mc², the relativistic momentum of photon is; p = mc,

blocks.prompt: 15 What is the momentum of a photon of wavelength 663 nm?

book_ref.quote: The beam of light with wavelength λ consists of a stream of photons travelling at speed c and carries energy; E = hf.

blocks.prompt: 16 Quantum theory can be extended to a mass oscillating on a spring, but its particle nature is not seen because:

options.text: its energy is not quantized at all
h is zero for large objects
it does not move fast enough
its energy steps are far too small to be detected

blocks.explanation: The energy steps of such a system are far too small to be detected, so any particle nature is invisible (18.1).

book_ref.quote: However, energy steps are far too small to be detected, so any particle nature is invisible.

blocks.prompt: 17 Quantum effects are important only when observing:
blocks.explanation: Quantum effects matter only for atom sized objects, where h is significant in any detectable energy change (18.1).

book_ref.quote: Quantum effects are only important when observing atom sized objects

blocks.prompt: 18 The photoelectric effect is the emission of:

options.text: light from a metal surface when it is heated
electrons from a metal surface exposed to light of suitable frequency
protons from a metal surface struck by light
electrons from a metal only when it is red hot

blocks.explanation: Photoelectric effect: emission of electrons from a metal surface exposed to light of suitable frequency or wavelength (18.2).

book_ref.quote: The process of emission of electrons from a metal surface when exposed to light of suitable frequency or wavelength is called the photoelectric effect.

blocks.prompt: 19 The electrons emitted in the photoelectric effect are called:
blocks.explanation: The emitted electrons are known as photoelectrons (18.2).

book_ref.quote: The emitted electrons are known as photoelectrons.

blocks.prompt: 20 In the apparatus of Fig. 18.1, monochromatic light of suitable frequency is made to shine on:

options.text: the cathode C connected to the negative terminal
the anode connected to the positive terminal
the glass wall of the tube

blocks.explanation: Electrode C, joined to the negative terminal, is the cathode; light on it emits electrons, which go to the positive anode (18.2).

book_ref.quote: The metal electrode C connected to negative terminal acts as cathode.

blocks.prompt: 21 In the photoelectric experiment the photoelectric current is measured by a:
blocks.explanation: The photoelectrons are attracted by the positive anode and the current is measured by a micro-ammeter (18.2).

book_ref.quote: These photoelectrons are attracted by the positive anode and the resulting current is measured by a micro-ammeter.

blocks.prompt: 22 In the photoelectric experiment the current stops as soon as the light is cut off. This proves that:

options.text: the battery alone drives the current
the tube is filled with gas
the current flows because of the incident light

blocks.explanation: Because the current stops when light is cut off, it flows due to the incident light; it is called photoelectric current (18.2).

book_ref.quote: The current stops when light is cut off, which proves that the current flows because of incident light.

blocks.prompt: 23 The stopping potential V₀ in the photoelectric experiment is:

options.text: the positive potential at which the current is maximum
the negative potential of the anode at which the photoelectric current becomes zero
the potential at which electrons first leave the cathode
the potential of the battery when the light is cut off

blocks.explanation: With connections reversed, the anode is made more and more negative; at the stopping potential V₀ even the most energetic electrons cannot reach it and the current becomes zero (18.2).

book_ref.quote: at a certain value, called stopping potential V₀, the current becomes zero

blocks.prompt: 24 The stopping potential for a metal surface is 1.5 V. The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is:

book_ref.quote: The maximum kinetic energy of photoelectrons is, thus

blocks.prompt: 25 Light of the same frequency but higher intensity falls on the cathode. Then:

options.text: the current stays the same but the stopping potential increases
the current increases but the stopping potential stays the same
both current and stopping potential increase
the current and stopping potential both decrease

blocks.explanation: Higher intensity increases the current, but the current stops at the same V₀ (Fig. 18.2, I₂ > I₁) (18.2).

book_ref.quote: If the experiment is repeated with light beam of higher intensity, the amount of current increases but the current stops for the same value of V₀.

blocks.prompt: 26 Intensity is kept constant and the frequency of incident light is changed. The curves of Fig. 18.3 show that:

options.text: the stopping potential is the same for every frequency
the current is zero for every frequency
the current is the same but the stopping potential is different for each frequency
the current increases but the stopping potential does not change

blocks.explanation: At constant intensity the current is the same but V₀ is different for each frequency, so (K.E.)max depends on frequency (18.2).

book_ref.quote: The current is same but stopping potential is different for each frequency of incident light

blocks.prompt: 27 The maximum energy of photoelectrons depends on:

options.text: the metal surface and the frequency of incident light
the time for which light falls
the area of the cathode only

blocks.explanation: (K.E.)max depends on the particular metal surface and the frequency of the incident light, not on intensity (18.2).

book_ref.quote: The maximum energy of photoelectrons depends on the particular metal surface and the frequency of incident light.

blocks.prompt: 28 Threshold frequency is the:

options.text: maximum frequency that a metal can absorb
frequency at which the current is largest
frequency at which the intensity becomes zero
minimum frequency below which no electrons are emitted, however intense the light

blocks.explanation: Below the threshold frequency no electrons are emitted, however intense the light may be (18.2).

book_ref.quote: There is a minimum frequency called threshold frequency below which no electrons are emitted

blocks.prompt: 29 When red light and blue light fall on sodium metal (Fig. 18.4):

options.text: blue light emits electrons but red light does not
red light emits electrons but blue light does not

blocks.explanation: Blue light produces photoelectric emission in sodium but red light, whose frequency is below threshold, does not (18.2).

book_ref.quote: For example, blue light produces photoelectric emission in sodium metal but red light does not

blocks.prompt: 30 The threshold frequency f₀:

options.text: is the same for all metals
depends on the intensity of light
depends on the area of the metal plate

blocks.explanation: f₀ varies from metal to metal (18.2), because each metal has its own work function, φ = hf₀.

book_ref.quote: This threshold frequency f₀ varies from metal to metal.

blocks.prompt: 31 In the photoelectric effect, the intensity of light (above threshold) determines:

options.text: the maximum kinetic energy of electrons
only the number of electrons emitted
the work function of the metal

blocks.explanation: Electrons are emitted instantaneously and the intensity determines only their number (18.2).

book_ref.quote: Electrons are emitted instantaneously; the intensity of light determines only their number.

blocks.prompt: 32 Photoelectric emission from a metal takes place only if the wavelength of the incident light is:
blocks.explanation: Emission needs f above f₀; since c = fλ, a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength, so λ must be shorter than the threshold wavelength (18.2).

book_ref.quote: The corresponding wavelength of incident light is called threshold wavelength.

blocks.prompt: 33 According to the electromagnetic wave theory of light, increasing the intensity of the incident light should:

options.text: decrease the number of emitted electrons
increase the kinetic energy of the emitted electrons

blocks.explanation: Wave theory predicts higher K.E. with higher intensity, which contradicts experiment; it also cannot explain the threshold frequency (18.2).

book_ref.quote: According to this theory, increasing the intensity of incident light should increase the K.E. of emitted electrons

blocks.prompt: 34 The work function φ of a metal is the:

options.text: maximum kinetic energy of a photoelectron
minimum energy an electron needs to escape from the metal surface

blocks.explanation: The work function φ is the minimum energy an electron needs to escape from the metal surface (18.2).

book_ref.quote: The electron needs a certain minimum energy called the work function φ to escape from the metal surface.

blocks.prompt: 35 Einstein's photoelectric equation is:
blocks.explanation: Incident photon energy − work function = (K.E.)max, i.e. hf − φ = ½mv²max (Eq. 18.5).

book_ref.quote: This is known as Einstein's photoelectric equation.

blocks.prompt: 36 The work function φ and threshold frequency f₀ of a metal are related by:
blocks.explanation: At the threshold (K.E.)max = 0, so hf₀ − φ = 0, i.e. φ = hf₀ (Eq. 18.6, with f₀ as in the book correction).

book_ref.quote: When (K.E.)max of the photoelectron is zero, the frequency f is equal to threshold frequency f₀

blocks.prompt: 37 All photoelectrons do not have the maximum kinetic energy because:

options.text: the light intensity varies with time
the work function changes during emission
some lose energy in atomic collisions before coming out

blocks.explanation: Some electrons come straight out, while others lose energy in atomic collisions; Eq. 18.7 holds only for those with full surplus energy (18.2).

book_ref.quote: some electrons come straight out of the metal surface and some lose energy in atomic collisions before coming out

blocks.prompt: 38 Albert Einstein was awarded the Nobel Prize in physics in 1921 for his:
blocks.explanation: Einstein received the 1921 Nobel Prize for his explanation of the photoelectric effect (18.2).

book_ref.quote: Albert Einstein was awarded Nobel Prize in physics in 1921 for his explanation of photoelectric effect.

blocks.prompt: 39 The photoelectric effect can be explained only by assuming that light:

options.text: is a wave with energy spread uniformly over its wavefront
consists of small packets of energy called photons

blocks.explanation: The effect cannot be explained if energy is spread uniformly over a wavefront; it needs photons, showing the particle nature of light (18.2).

book_ref.quote: Thus, it shows the particle nature of light.

blocks.prompt: 40 The work function of a metal is 2.0 eV. Its threshold frequency is:

book_ref.quote: The electron needs a certain minimum energy called the work function φ to escape from the metal surface.

blocks.prompt: 41 The threshold wavelength of a metal of work function 3.0 eV is about:

book_ref.quote: When (K.E.)max of the photoelectron is zero, the frequency f is equal to threshold frequency f₀

blocks.prompt: 42 Photons of energy 4.0 eV fall on a metal of work function 2.5 eV. The stopping potential is:
blocks.explanation: (K.E.)max = hf − φ = 4.0 − 2.5 = 1.5 eV; since (K.E.)max = V₀e, V₀ = 1.5 V (Eqs. 18.4, 18.5).

book_ref.quote: A part of the photon energy is used by the electron to break away from the metal and the rest appears as the kinetic energy of the electron.

blocks.prompt: 43 Light of wavelength 400 nm falls on a metal of work function 2.0 eV. The maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is about:

book_ref.quote: A part of the photon energy is used by the electron to break away from the metal and the rest appears as the kinetic energy of the electron.

blocks.prompt: 44 The energy of a photon of light of wavelength 500 nm is about:

book_ref.quote: Find the energy of a photon in eV of the blue light of wavelength 450 nm.

blocks.prompt: 45 A graph of (K.E.)max of photoelectrons against the frequency f of light (Eq. 18.7) is a straight line whose slope is:
blocks.explanation: (K.E.)max = hf − hf₀: plotted against f this is a line of slope h that meets the frequency axis at f₀ (Eq. 18.7).

book_ref.quote: Hence, we can also write Einstein's photoelectric equation as

blocks.prompt: 46 On the graph of (K.E.)max against light frequency, no photoemission occurs for frequencies:
blocks.explanation: Below the threshold frequency f₀ no photoemission occurs (graph in the 'For your information' box, 18.2).

book_ref.quote: Below a certain frequency fo, no photoemission occurs

blocks.prompt: 47 Photons of energy 2.6 eV eject electrons from a metal and the stopping potential is 0.6 V. The work function of the metal is:
blocks.explanation: (K.E.)max = V₀e = 0.6 eV; φ = hf − (K.E.)max = 2.6 − 0.6 = 2.0 eV (as in Example 18.2).

book_ref.quote: Yellow light of 577 nm wavelength is incident on a cesium metal surface.

blocks.prompt: 48 When electromagnetic radiation of low energy (less than 0.5 MeV) interacts with matter, the dominant process is:
blocks.explanation: Below 0.5 MeV photoelectric effect dominates; at intermediate energies Compton effect; above 1.2 MeV pair production (box, 18.2).

book_ref.quote: (i) At low energies (less than 0.5 MeV), the dominant process is photoelectric effect.

blocks.prompt: 49 For photons of energy more than 1.2 MeV interacting with matter, the dominant process is:
blocks.explanation: At higher energies (more than 1.2 MeV) the dominant process is pair production (box, 18.2).

book_ref.quote: (iii) At higher energies (more than 1.2MeV), the dominant process is pair production.

blocks.prompt: 50 At intermediate photon energies, the dominant interaction of electromagnetic radiation with matter is:
blocks.explanation: At intermediate energies the dominant process is Compton effect (box, 18.2).

book_ref.quote: (ii) At intermediate energies, the dominant process is Compton effect.

blocks.prompt: 51 In 1923 Compton studied the scattering of X-rays by:

options.text: loosely bound electrons of a graphite target

blocks.explanation: Compton studied X-rays scattered by loosely bound electrons from a graphite target (18.3, Fig. 18.5).

book_ref.quote: studied the scattering of X-rays by loosely bound electrons from a graphite target

blocks.prompt: 52 In the Compton effect, the wavelength of the scattered X-rays is:

options.text: smaller than that of the incident X-rays
equal to that of the incident X-rays
larger than that of the incident X-rays

blocks.explanation: Compton found λs of the scattered X-rays larger than λi of the incident X-rays (18.3).

book_ref.quote: He found that wavelength λs, of the scattered X-rays is larger than the wavelength λi of the incident X-rays.

blocks.prompt: 53 The increase in wavelength of scattered X-rays could NOT be explained on the basis of:
blocks.explanation: The increase in wavelength could not be explained by classical wave theory; Compton used photons with energy hc/λ and momentum h/λ (18.3).

book_ref.quote: The increase in wavelength of scattered X-rays could not be explained on the basis of classical wave theory.

blocks.prompt: 54 To explain his result, Compton suggested that X-rays consist of photons with:
blocks.explanation: Compton suggested X-rays are photons with energy hc/λ and momentum h/λ (18.3).

book_ref.quote: Compton suggested that X-rays consist of photons with energy hc/λ and momentum h/λ.

blocks.prompt: 55 In deriving the Compton shift, the collision of the X-ray photon with the electron is treated as:

options.text: an elastic collision in which both energy and momentum are conserved
an inelastic collision in which only momentum is conserved
a collision in which only energy is conserved
a collision in which neither is conserved

blocks.explanation: It is treated like the elastic collision of two balls; both energy and momentum are conserved (18.3).

book_ref.quote: Actually this is simple problem of the elastic collision of two balls. Both energy and momentum are conserved.

blocks.prompt: 56 In the Compton effect, the kinetic energy of the recoiling electron is:
blocks.explanation: K.E. of the electron = total energy after collision (mc²) − before collision (m₀c²) = (m − m₀)c² (18.3).

book_ref.quote: with K.E. equal to (m − m₀)c²

blocks.prompt: 57 In the Compton derivation, momentum is conserved separately along x and y because:
blocks.explanation: Momentum is a vector, so it must be conserved for both x and y components (18.3).

book_ref.quote: Since momentum is a vector quantity, it must be conserved both for x and y-components.

blocks.prompt: 58 The Compton shift in wavelength is given by:
blocks.explanation: Δλ = λ′ − λ = (h/m₀c)(1 − cos θ) (Eq. 18.8).

book_ref.quote: Let us derive an expression for change in wavelength Δλ known as Compton shift in wavelength.

blocks.prompt: 59 The Compton wavelength h/m₀c of the electron has the value:

book_ref.quote: The factor h/m₀c has dimensions of wavelength and is called Compton wavelength and has the numerical value

blocks.prompt: 60 For X-rays scattered at θ = 90°, the Compton shift:
blocks.explanation: At 90°, cos θ = 0, so Δλ = h/m₀c, the Compton wavelength (18.3).

book_ref.quote: If the scattered X-ray photons are observed at θ = 90°, the Compton shift Δλ equals the Compton wavelength.

blocks.prompt: 61 The Compton shift for X-rays scattered at 60° from a target of loosely bound electrons is about:

book_ref.quote: The factor h/m₀c has dimensions of wavelength and is called Compton wavelength and has the numerical value

blocks.prompt: 62 The Compton shift is maximum when the scattering angle θ is:
blocks.explanation: 1 − cos θ is largest (= 2) at θ = 180°: Δλ = 2 × 2.43 pm = 4.86 pm (Eq. 18.8).

book_ref.quote: Let us derive an expression for change in wavelength Δλ known as Compton shift in wavelength.

book_ref.quote: By solving the above equation, it is found that relation between original wavelength λ of photon

blocks.prompt: 64 X-rays scattered straight ahead (θ = 0°) in the Compton effect show a shift of:
blocks.explanation: At θ = 0°, cos θ = 1 and Δλ = (h/m₀c)(1 − 1) = 0 (Eq. 18.8).

book_ref.quote: By solving the above equation, it is found that relation between original wavelength λ of photon

blocks.prompt: 65 The agreement of the Compton shift equation with Compton's experimental results confirms:

options.text: the particle like interaction of electromagnetic waves with matter

blocks.explanation: Agreement with experiment is a striking confirmation of the particle like interaction of electromagnetic waves with matter (18.3).

book_ref.quote: which again is a striking confirmation of particle like interaction of electromagnetic waves with matter

blocks.prompt: 66 Arthur Holly Compton was awarded the Nobel Prize in physics in:
blocks.explanation: Compton received the Nobel Prize in 1927 for the effect named after him (18.3).

book_ref.quote: Arthur Holly Compton was awarded Nobel Prize in physics in 1927

blocks.prompt: 67 In pair production, a very high energy photon is changed into:
blocks.explanation: In pair production the photon energy is changed into an electron-positron pair (18.3).

book_ref.quote: It is pair production in which photon energy is changed into electron-positron pair

blocks.prompt: 68 The converse of pair production is known as:
blocks.explanation: The converse of pair production is annihilation of matter, in which a particle and its antiparticle become γ-ray photons (18.3).

book_ref.quote: the converse of pair-production is known as annihilation of matter

blocks.prompt: 69 When an electron and a positron annihilate, the result is:

options.text: two high energy photons in the γ-ray range

blocks.explanation: e⁻ + e⁺ = γ + γ: a particle and its antiparticle annihilate into high energy γ-ray photons (18.3).

book_ref.quote: a particle and its antiparticle interact and annihilate into high energy photons in the γ-rays range

blocks.prompt: 70 The rest mass energy of an electron (and of a positron) is 0.51 MeV. A photon of 3.02 MeV produces an electron-positron pair. The total kinetic energy of the pair is:

book_ref.quote: We have already discussed in previous class, another kind of very high energy photon

blocks.prompt: 71 The idea that material particles should possess wave-like properties was proposed in 1924 by:
blocks.explanation: Assuming symmetry in nature, Louis de Broglie proposed in 1924 that particles possess wave-like properties (18.4).

book_ref.quote: Louis de Broglie proposed in 1924 that particles should also possess wave-like properties

blocks.prompt: 72 de Broglie's proposal that particles have waves was based on:

options.text: the failure of the photoelectric effect
symmetry in nature, since light shows a dual nature

blocks.explanation: Light shows a dual nature; assuming symmetry in nature, de Broglie proposed that particles also have wave-like properties (18.4).

book_ref.quote: Assuming symmetry in nature, the French physicist, Louis de Broglie proposed in 1924

blocks.prompt: 73 The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass m moving with velocity v is:
blocks.explanation: p = h/λ = mv gives λ = h/p = h/mv (Eq. 18.10, p as in the book correction).

book_ref.quote: de Broglie suggested that momentum of a material particle of mass m moving with velocity v should be given by the same expression.

blocks.prompt: 74 The de Broglie wavelength of an electron (m = 9.1 × 10⁻³¹ kg) moving with speed 2 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ is about:

book_ref.quote: On the other hands, for an electron moving with a speed of 1 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹:

blocks.prompt: 75 The de Broglie wavelength of a ball of mass 0.1 kg moving at 10 m s⁻¹ is:
blocks.explanation: λ = h/mv = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/(0.1 × 10) = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ m: far too small for any wave effect to be noticed (18.4).

book_ref.quote: An object of large mass and ordinary speed has such a small wavelength that its wave effects such as interference and diffraction are negligible.

blocks.prompt: 76 If the speed of a particle is doubled (mass unchanged), its de Broglie wavelength:
blocks.explanation: λ = h/mv, so λ ∝ 1/v; doubling v halves λ (Eq. 18.10).

book_ref.quote: An object of large mass and ordinary speed has such a small wavelength that its wave effects such as interference and diffraction are negligible.

blocks.prompt: 77 The de Broglie wavelength of an electron moving at 1 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹ (about 7 × 10⁻¹⁰ m) lies in the range of:
blocks.explanation: λ ≈ 7 × 10⁻¹⁰ m is in the X-rays range, so diffraction effects for electrons are measurable (18.4).

book_ref.quote: This wavelength is in the X-rays range.

blocks.prompt: 78 An electron-positron pair at rest annihilates into two photons. The energy carried by each photon is:

options.text: zero, since photons have no mass
0.51 MeV, the rest mass energy of an electron

blocks.explanation: 0.51 MeV is the rest mass energy of the electron and of the positron; each photon carries 0.51 MeV (Example 18.3, book correction).

book_ref.quote: Find the wavelength of two photons produced when a positron-electron pair annihilates.

blocks.prompt: 79 Davisson and Germer showed that electrons:

options.text: are diffracted from metal crystals just like X-rays
are emitted from metals by light

blocks.explanation: Davisson and Germer showed electrons are diffracted from metal crystals in exactly the same manner as X-rays (18.4).

book_ref.quote: They showed that electrons are diffracted from metal crystals in exactly the same manner as X-rays or any other wave.

blocks.prompt: 80 In the Davisson-Germer experiment the electron beam was made incident on a crystal of:
blocks.explanation: The accelerated electron beam was incident on a nickel crystal (18.4, Fig. 18.7).

book_ref.quote: The electron beam is then made incident on a nickel crystal.

blocks.prompt: 81 Davisson and Germer interpreted the regular peaks of scattered electrons as a result of:
blocks.explanation: The scattered electrons came off in regular peaks, interpreted as diffraction just like X-ray diffraction by an NaCl crystal (18.4).

book_ref.quote: The scattered electrons from metal surface came off in regular peaks.

blocks.prompt: 82 The de Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated from rest through a potential difference V is:
blocks.explanation: ½mv² = Ve gives mv = √(2mVe), and λ = h/mv = h/√(2mVe) (Eq. 18.11).

book_ref.quote: The gain in K.E. of the electron as it is accelerated by a potential V in the electron gun is given by

book_ref.quote: In one of the experiments, the accelerating voltage V was 54 volts, hence,

blocks.prompt: 84 If the accelerating voltage of an electron is made four times, its de Broglie wavelength becomes:
blocks.explanation: λ = h/√(2mVe), so λ ∝ 1/√V; V × 4 gives λ ÷ 2 (Eq. 18.11).

book_ref.quote: In one of the experiments, the accelerating voltage V was 54 volts, hence,

blocks.prompt: 85 In the Davisson-Germer experiment, the experimental wavelength of the electrons was found from:
blocks.explanation: The diffracted beam at a glancing angle of 65° gave λ through Bragg's equation 2d sin θ = mλ, agreeing with h/√(2mVe) (18.4).

book_ref.quote: This beam of electrons diffracted from crystal surface was obtained for a glancing angle of 65°.

blocks.prompt: 86 Besides electrons, diffraction patterns have also been observed with:

options.text: protons, neutrons, hydrogen atoms and helium atoms

blocks.explanation: Diffraction has also been observed with protons, neutrons, hydrogen and helium atoms, evidence for the wave nature of particles (18.4).

book_ref.quote: Diffraction patterns have also been observed with protons, neutrons, hydrogen atoms and helium atoms

blocks.prompt: 87 The Nobel Prize of 1937 for the experimental confirmation of the wave nature of particles was shared by:

options.text: C. J. Davisson and G. P. Thomson
L. de Broglie and M. Planck
A. H. Compton and A. Einstein

blocks.explanation: Davisson and G. P. Thomson shared the 1937 prize; de Broglie had received the 1929 prize (18.4).

book_ref.quote: Clinton Joseph Davisson and George Paget Thomson shared the Nobel Prize in 1937

blocks.prompt: 88 Louis de Broglie received the Nobel Prize in physics for his work on the dual nature of particles in:
blocks.explanation: de Broglie received the 1929 Nobel Prize (18.4); 1924 is the year of his proposal.

book_ref.quote: Prince Louis Victor de Broglie received the 1929 Nobel Prize in physics

blocks.prompt: 89 Which pair of phenomena proves the particle nature of light?
blocks.explanation: Interference and diffraction show the wave nature; photoelectric and Compton effects prove the particle nature of light (18.5).

book_ref.quote: while photoelectric effect and Compton effect prove the particle nature of light

blocks.prompt: 90 In J. J. Thomson's experiment to find e/m, the electron had to be treated as:
blocks.explanation: In J. J. Thomson's e/m experiment the particle-like nature of the electron had to be assumed (18.5).

book_ref.quote: in the experiment of J. J. Thomson to find e/m, we had to assume particle-like nature of the electron

blocks.prompt: 91 The principle of complementarity, that both wave and particle aspects are needed for a complete description, was stated by:
blocks.explanation: Niels Bohr's principle of complementarity: both wave and particle aspects are required for a complete description of radiation and matter (18.5).

book_ref.quote: Niels Bohr pointed out in stating his principle of complementarity

blocks.prompt: 92 According to the principle of complementarity, the wave and particle aspects of light:

options.text: cannot both be revealed simultaneously in a single experiment
are always revealed together in every experiment

blocks.explanation: Both aspects are always present, but they cannot be revealed simultaneously in a single experiment (18.5).

book_ref.quote: However, both aspects cannot be revealed simultaneously in a single experiment.

blocks.prompt: 93 A diffraction grating is placed in the path of a light beam. The light is then revealed as:

options.text: both a wave and a particle at once

blocks.explanation: A diffraction grating reveals light as a wave; the aspect seen depends on the experiment (18.5).

book_ref.quote: If we put a diffraction grating in the path of a light beam, we reveal it as a wave.

blocks.prompt: 94 Whether light shows its wave aspect or particle aspect is determined by:

options.text: the colour of the light only
the nature of the experiment being done
the observer's distance from the source

blocks.explanation: The two aspects are different 'faces' of light; a particular aspect is determined by the nature of the experiment (18.5).

book_ref.quote: A particular aspect is determined by the nature of the experiment being done.

blocks.prompt: 95 According to wave-particle duality, micro-particles such as electrons and photons:

options.text: propagate as waves and exchange energies as particles
propagate as particles and exchange energies as waves

blocks.explanation: All micro-particles propagate as if they were waves and exchange energies as if they were particles (18.5).

book_ref.quote: all micro-particles (electrons, protons, photons, atoms, etc.) propagate as if they were waves and exchange energies as if they were particles

blocks.prompt: 96 A beam of electrons is passed through a double slit. In reality the screen shows:

options.text: two exact images of the slits only
a pattern of bright and dark fringes
a uniform glow with no pattern

blocks.explanation: Particles alone would give two images of the slits; in reality the screen shows bright and dark fringes, as with light (Do you know?, 18.5).

book_ref.quote: In reality, the screen reveals a pattern of bright and dark fringes

blocks.prompt: 97 The experiments of Davisson and Germer and of G. P. Thomson reveal:
blocks.explanation: The Davisson-Germer and G. P. Thomson experiments reveal the wave-like nature of electrons (18.5).

book_ref.quote: the experiments of Davisson and Germer and G. P. Thomson reveal wave-like nature of electrons

blocks.prompt: 98 The de Broglie wavelength of the electrons used in an electron microscope, compared with the wavelength of visible light, is about:
blocks.explanation: The electrons' de Broglie wavelength is about a thousand times shorter than that of visible light, so finer details are seen (18.6).

book_ref.quote: Electron microscope uses the wave nature of electrons whose de Broglie wavelength is thousand times

blocks.prompt: 99 In an electron microscope, the lens that focuses the electron beam on the specimen is the:
blocks.explanation: Electrons pass through the electromagnetic condenser lens, which focuses the beam on the specimen (18.6).

book_ref.quote: The electrons from a source are passed through the electromagnetic lens called condenser

blocks.prompt: 100 In an electron microscope, the image of the specimen is formed by the:
blocks.explanation: The electromagnetic objective lens forms the image of the specimen; the projector lens then magnifies it (18.6).

book_ref.quote: An electromagnetic lens (objective lens) form the image of specimen.

blocks.prompt: 101 The photograph of the image produced on film in an electron microscope is called a:
blocks.explanation: The projector lens magnifies the image to photograph it on a film, called a micrograph (18.6).

book_ref.quote: The image is further magnified by the electromagnetic projector lens to photograph the image on a film, called micrograph.

blocks.prompt: 102 In an electron microscope, increasing the speed of the electrons:

options.text: shortens their wavelength and increases the resolution
lengthens their wavelength and increases the resolution
shortens their wavelength and decreases the resolution

blocks.explanation: Higher speed gives shorter wavelength and hence higher resolution (18.6).

book_ref.quote: The higher is the speed of electrons, the shorter is the wavelength and hence, higher is the resolution.

blocks.prompt: 103 A three dimensional image of remarkable quality is obtained with a:
blocks.explanation: Modern versions called scanning electron microscopes give three dimensional images of remarkable quality (18.6).

book_ref.quote: A three dimensional image of remarkable quality can be achieved by modern versions called scanning electron microscopes.

blocks.prompt: 104 Which of the following is a use of the electron microscope given in the chapter?
blocks.explanation: Uses: study of cell structure, viruses and bacteria, metal fractures, materials and crystal structure (18.6).

book_ref.quote: The uses include study of cell structure, viruses and bacteria in microbiology

blocks.prompt: 105 An electron microscope can see details down to about the:

options.text: level of a human hair only

blocks.explanation: An electron microscope sees details down to the nano-metric, about atomic, level (18.6).

book_ref.quote: As stated above, electron microscope can see much smaller details down to nano-metric

blocks.prompt: 106 The experimental arrangement for observing atomic spectra (Fig. 18.9) consists of:

options.text: an X-ray tube, a graphite block and a detector
a photocell, a battery and a micro-ammeter
a discharge tube, a spectrometer and a diffraction grating
an electron gun and a nickel crystal

blocks.explanation: Atomic spectra are observed with a discharge tube, spectrometer and diffraction grating (18.7).

book_ref.quote: The experimental arrangement consists of a discharge tube, spectrometer and diffraction grating

blocks.prompt: 107 Spectral series of the vapours of different elements can be used to:
blocks.explanation: Each element's vapour shows its own pattern of lines (spectral series), which identifies the element (18.7).

book_ref.quote: The vapours of different elements exhibit different patterns of such lines called spectral series which can be used to identify different elements.

blocks.prompt: 116 The longest wavelength of the Paschen series (n = 4 to n = 3) is about:

book_ref.quote: This series is known as Paschen series.

blocks.prompt: 117 In the hydrogen atom, the state n = 1 is called the:
blocks.explanation: n = 1 is the ground state; n = 2, 3, 4, ... are excited states (18.7).

book_ref.quote: The state for n = 1 is said to be the ground state whereas the state n = 2, 3, 4, ... are called excited states.

blocks.prompt: 118 An electron raised to an excited state of a hydrogen atom:

options.text: soon returns to a lower level, emitting photons
leaves the atom as a photoelectron

blocks.explanation: Excited states have very short life; the electron soon returns to a lower level by emitting photons, seen as the emission spectrum (18.7).

book_ref.quote: The excited states have very short life.

blocks.prompt: 119 White light passed through a gas at low pressure shows dark lines in its spectrum. This is a/an:
blocks.explanation: Missing wavelengths appear as dark lines; this is an absorption spectrum (18.7).

book_ref.quote: In their places dark lines are seen. This type of spectrum is called absorption spectrum.

blocks.prompt: 120 When white light passes through a gas, the gas atoms absorb:

options.text: only photons of certain energies or frequencies

blocks.explanation: Only photons of certain energy are absorbed, matching exactly the energy needed for upward transitions (18.7).

book_ref.quote: Only photons of certain energy or frequency are absorbed.

blocks.prompt: 121 The wavelengths missing from the absorption line spectrum of an element are:

options.text: absent from its emission spectrum too
the same as those present in its emission line spectrum
different for every sample of the element

blocks.explanation: Wavelengths missing from the absorption spectrum are those present in the emission spectrum of the same element (18.7, Fig. 18.13).

book_ref.quote: It means the wavelengths missing from an absorption line spectrum are those present in the emission line spectrum

blocks.prompt: 122 To excite a gas atom between two levels, a photon must have energy:

options.text: exactly equal to the energy difference, but an electron needs K.E. greater than or equal to it
greater than or equal to the difference, but an electron needs exactly equal
exactly equal to the difference, and so must an electron
any value, for both photon and electron

blocks.explanation: A photon must have exactly the energy difference; an electron with K.E. greater than or equal to it can excite the atom (Do you know?, 18.7).

book_ref.quote: Photon must have energy exactly equal to the energy difference between the two shells for excitation of an atom

book_ref.quote: This transition of energy is equl to; hf = Eₙ − Eₚ.

blocks.prompt: 124 The three types of spectra named in the chapter are:

options.text: visible, ultraviolet and infrared spectra only

blocks.explanation: The box names continuous, line and band spectra (18.7). Lyman, Balmer and Paschen are series of the hydrogen line spectrum.

book_ref.quote: Different types of spectra: continuous spectrum, line spectrum and band spectrum

blocks.prompt: 125 According to the uncertainty principle, the quantities that cannot be measured simultaneously with perfect accuracy are:

options.text: position and momentum of a particle
mass and charge of a particle
speed and direction of a photon in vacuum

blocks.explanation: Position and momentum of a particle cannot be measured simultaneously with perfect accuracy (18.8).

book_ref.quote: Position and momentum of a particle cannot be measured simultaneously with perfect accuracy.

blocks.prompt: 126 The fundamental uncertainty in measuring position and momentum arises from:

options.text: the wave-particle duality of matter and radiation

blocks.explanation: The uncertainty is not due to the instrument; it is a consequence of wave-particle duality (18.8).

book_ref.quote: This uncertainty is not associated with the measuring instrument.

blocks.prompt: 127 The uncertainty principle was first proposed in 1927 by:
blocks.explanation: Werner Heisenberg first proposed it in 1927, hence the Heisenberg uncertainty principle (18.8).

book_ref.quote: This was first proposed by Werner Heisenberg in 1927

blocks.prompt: 128 The uncertainty principle is negligible for a flying tennis ball but important for an electron because:

options.text: electrons cannot be struck by photons
photons hardly affect the ball's path but one photon drastically alters an electron's motion
the ball moves faster than light

blocks.explanation: Photons striking a tennis ball hardly affect its path, but one photon striking an electron drastically alters its motion (18.8).

book_ref.quote: a stream of light photons striking a flying tennis ball hardly affects its path, but one photon striking an electron drastically alters its motion

blocks.prompt: 129 If light of wavelength λ is used to locate a micro-particle, the uncertainty in its position is about:
blocks.explanation: Position can be found only to within one wavelength: Δx ≈ λ (18.8).

book_ref.quote: we would expect to be able to determine the position of the electron only to within one wavelength of the light being used

blocks.prompt: 130 When light of wavelength λ locates a micro-particle, the uncertainty in the particle's momentum is about:
blocks.explanation: At most the photon transfers all its momentum h/λ, so Δp ≈ h/λ (18.8).

book_ref.quote: At most, the photon of light can transfer all its momentum h/λ to the micro-particle

blocks.prompt: 131 Using light of shorter wavelength to locate an electron:

options.text: increases Δx but makes momentum exact
reduces Δx but makes the momentum measurement less precise

blocks.explanation: Shorter λ gives a smaller Δx ≈ λ, but the photon alters the motion drastically, so Δp ≈ h/λ becomes larger (18.8).

book_ref.quote: But it will alter the motion drastically making momentum measurement less precise.

blocks.prompt: 132 The position-momentum uncertainty principle (Eq. 18.14) is:
blocks.explanation: Multiplying Δx ≈ λ and Δp ≈ h/λ gives Δx.Δp ≈ h (Eq. 18.14).

book_ref.quote: approximately equals Planck's constant h

blocks.explanation: Δp ≈ h/Δx = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴/2 × 10⁻¹⁰ = 3.3 × 10⁻²⁴ kg m s⁻¹; momentum is in kg m s⁻¹, not J s (18.8, book correction).

book_ref.quote: Equation 18.14 is the mathematical form of position-momentum uncertainty principle.

book_ref.quote: The corresponding energy uncertainty should be of the order of GeV.

blocks.prompt: 137 According to the energy-time uncertainty principle, the more accurately the energy of a particle is determined:

options.text: the more uncertain is the time during which it has that energy
the more exactly its time is also known

blocks.explanation: ΔE.Δt ≈ h: the more accurately the energy is found, the more uncertain the time during which the particle has it (18.8).

book_ref.quote: Thus, more accurately we determined the energy of a particle, the more uncertain we will be of the time during which it has that energy.

blocks.prompt: 139 Werner Heisenberg was awarded the Nobel Prize for his contribution to quantum physics in:
blocks.explanation: Heisenberg received the Nobel Prize in 1932 (18.8); 1927 is when he proposed the uncertainty principle.

book_ref.quote: Heisenberg was awarded Nobel Prize in 1932 for his contribution towards quantum physics.

blocks.prompt: 140 Which statement about the sub-atomic world is given in the chapter?

options.text: Position has no meaning at all
Few things can be predicted with 100% precision

blocks.explanation: In the sub-atomic world few things can be predicted with 100% precision (Do you know?, 18.8).

book_ref.quote: In the sub-atomic world, few things can be predicted with 100% precision.
